planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; as with the straight species, it tolerates poorly drained, swampy ground better than most narrow evergreens.

directions: Top Point is a slow-growing, distinctly narrow and upright dwarf selection of the native Atlantic white cedar, holding a tight, columnar silhouette rather than the broader pyramid of seedling-grown trees. Give it full sun and reliably moist, acidic soil, since like the wild species it hails from coastal bogs and swamp forests and resents dry, alkaline sites. Its tight habit makes it useful as a living screen or vertical accent in rain gardens and wet borders where space is limited, and it needs little to no pruning to keep its form. Established plants tolerate occasional standing water far better than most upright evergreens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; established plants are quite drought-tolerant and resent heavy, wet ground.

directions: This compact, low, prostrate selection of the circumboreal native common juniper is grown for its abundant crop of powdery blue, berry-like cones set against fine, prickly blue-green needles. It stays considerably shorter and tighter than seedling common juniper, making it a practical choice for rock gardens, slopes, and foundation plantings where a sprawling conifer would overwhelm the space. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; once established it shrugs off drought, poor soil, and winter cold with little care. Avoid consistently wet sites, which can lead to root and foliage disease.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; this old cultivar tolerates poor, dry, and alkaline ground once established.

directions: Burkii is a long-grown, narrowly pyramidal selection of the native eastern red cedar prized for steel-blue to silvery foliage that shifts to a plummy purple-tinged bronze through winter cold. It holds a tighter, more formal outline than wild-type trees, making it a popular choice for windbreaks, screens, and specimen plantings in difficult, exposed sites. Like the species it thrives in poor, rocky, or alkaline soils and full sun, and once rooted in it needs almost no supplemental water. Its dense evergreen structure and berry-like blue cones also provide excellent winter cover and food for birds.
sources: Michael Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in reliably moist to wet soil; this trademarked selection grows to a similar full size as seedling buttonbush, so give it room at a pond margin or large rain garden.

directions: Crimson Comet is a named buttonbush selection grown for a strong seasonal show: clusters of fragrant, round white pincushion flowers open through mid to late summer, drawing a heavy traffic of bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds before giving way to persistent seed balls that feed waterfowl and songbirds into winter. Like all buttonbush, it tolerates standing water and seasonal flooding better than almost any other flowering shrub, so it is well suited to pond edges, bioswales, and low spots that stay damp, and it reaches a full, rounded size similar to the wild species rather than staying compact. Prune in late winter if a tighter form is wanted, since flowers form on new growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in lean, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; this nitrogen-fixing native shrub struggles in rich garden loam and overly wet ground.

directions: Blue Sea (sold under the NativeStar brand) is a selection of the native sweetfern grown for its narrow, fern-textured leaves carrying a more pronounced blue-green cast than the typical green-leaved species. Crush the foliage to release its sweet, resinous fragrance, a trademark of this nitrogen-fixing shrub that lets it thrive in poor, sandy, infertile soil where little else grows. It spreads gradually by underground runners to knit together a patch over time, making it a good low-maintenance choice for dry banks, sandy slopes, and naturalized plantings rather than tidy foundation beds. Avoid rich or constantly moist soil, which encourages weak, floppy growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; once established it is highly drought-tolerant and needs little supplemental irrigation.

directions: Originally found on San Bruno Mountain, this selection of California coffeeberry stays low and wide, mounding noticeably wider than tall rather than growing fully upright like the species, making it a dependable evergreen groundcover for slopes, banks, and erosion control in dry gardens. Leathery, glossy leaves stay attractive year-round, and small greenish flowers in late spring give way to berries that ripen from green through red to black, feeding birds over a long season. It asks only for well-drained soil and takes full coastal sun or light inland shade, needing little water once its roots are established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; space generously, since this is a more vigorous, larger-leaved selection than dwarf coffeeberry cultivars.

directions: Named for the California horticulturist who selected it, Eve Case is a vigorous, rounded form of coffeeberry with noticeably larger, glossier leaves than the straight species, giving it a lush, almost tropical look despite being thoroughly drought-tolerant once rooted in. Its dense, upright growth makes it one of the most popular native choices for informal evergreen hedges, screens, and background plantings in California gardens. Small flowers draw pollinators in spring, followed by a heavy crop of berries that ripen through shades of red to black and are a reliable food source for birds. Give it full sun near the coast or a bit of afternoon shade inland, and well-drained soil to avoid root disease.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; deerberry tolerates drier soil than most Vaccinium species.

directions: Deerberry is an underused native blueberry relative, and this compact selection keeps the species' charming spring display of small, bell-shaped white flowers with long, prominently exserted anthers that give the open blooms a starry, shooting-star look. Tart, blue-green to purple berries ripen in late summer and are readily eaten by birds, deer, and other wildlife, though they are more astringent raw than a cultivated blueberry. Unlike many Vaccinium species it tolerates drier, well-drained, acidic soils and part shade, making it a good fit for woodland edges and dry understory plantings rather than boggy ground. Its more compact size suits smaller native gardens where full-size deerberry would be too large.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall; avoid planting during peak summer heat to let roots establish.

directions: Chroma Chameleon is a purple-leaved ninebark selection that holds strong foliage color throughout the growing season, giving the shrub consistent impact rather than fading to green by midsummer as some older purple cultivars do. Domed clusters of small white to pale pink flowers appear in late spring against the colorful foliage, followed by reddish seed capsules that add fall interest. Like other ninebarks it is tough and adaptable, tolerating poor soil, heat, and drought once established, and its peeling, multicolored bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Full sun brings out the strongest foliage color; prune right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: This smooth hydrangea selection produces lacecap-style flower heads where a flat disk of tiny, pastel-pink fertile florets is ringed by the larger white sterile florets typical of the species, giving each flower head a subtle pink-and-white banded look rather than the solid mophead form most gardeners expect from Hydrangea arborescens. Like other smooth hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter without sacrificing the coming season's flowers. Plant in moist, humus-rich soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates to keep flowers from fading quickly, and the open lacecap form is particularly attractive to pollinators that can easily reach the fertile florets. Its native parentage makes it tougher and more adaptable to average garden soil than many introduced hydrangea species.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, average to wet soil; tolerates full sun to full shade and adapts to both wet and average garden conditions.

directions: True to its name, this Virginia sweetspire selection carries 4-6 inch fragrant white flower racemes that cascade from the arching branches in early summer like small fountains, followed by some of the most vivid fall color in the genus, with foliage turning deep wine-red to burgundy. Like the species it is remarkably adaptable, tolerating wet low spots, average garden soil, dry clay, and anything from full sun to full shade, though the richest fall color and heaviest bloom come with more sun. Plants spread gradually by suckers to form a loose colony over time, which can be left to naturalize a slope or wet margin or kept in check by removing wayward shoots. It is an easy, low-maintenance choice for borders, rain gardens, and foundation plantings alike.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; spicebush is dioecious, so a male plant must grow nearby for this female selection to set fruit.

directions: Scarlet Lady is a female spicebush selection chosen specifically for its heavy, reliable crop of glossy scarlet berries, solving the usual gamble of growing seed-raised spicebush and not knowing its sex until it either fruits or doesn't. Tiny yellow flowers open along the bare stems in early spring ahead of the leaves, an important early nectar source for queen bumblebees, and the berries that follow in fall are quickly stripped by thrushes, catbirds, and other songbirds. Like the species, its leaves, twigs, and fruit carry a strong allspice-like fragrance when crushed, and it serves as the required host plant for spicebush swallowtail caterpillars. Site it in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, with a male spicebush planted within pollinating distance to ensure fruit set.
